:::{#thm-linear-map-zero}
#### A linear map sends zero to zero

If $f: \reals^p \to \reals^m$ is a linear map (@def-linear-map),
then $f(\vzero) = \vzero$.

:::

::: proof

On the left, $\vzero$ is the zero vector of length $p$;
on the right, it is the zero vector of length $m$.

$$
\ba
f(\vzero)
&= f(0 \cd \vzero)
&& \text{(every entry of } 0 \cd \vzero \text{ is } 0 \cd 0 = 0 \text{; @def-scalar-mult)}
\\&= 0 \cd f(\vzero)
&& \text{(homogeneity, with } c = 0 \text{ and } \vx = \vzero \text{)}
\\&= \vzero
&& \text{(every entry of } 0 \cd f(\vzero) \text{ is } 0 \text{; @def-scalar-mult)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-linear-map-zero}
#### Ruling out linearity at zero

In @exm-linear-map, $g(x) = x + 1$ has $g(0) = 1 \neq 0$,
so by @thm-linear-map-zero it is not linear,
without checking additivity or homogeneity.

Sending $\vzero$ to $\vzero$ is necessary but not sufficient:
$h(x) = x^2$ in the same example has $h(0) = 0$
and is still not linear.

:::
